text: Lucy, the 3.2-million-year-old fossilized skeleton of a small bipedal creature, was found in Ethiopia in 1974. Scientists have long debated whether Lucy spent time in trees (arborealism) as well as on the ground. University of Texas researchers say the pattern of fractures seen in Lucy’s fossilized bones show that she died as the result of a “vertical deceleration event” The researchers estimate that Lucy was going about 35 miles an hour when she hit the ground after falling from a height of roughly 40 feet, according to the statement. But other scientists are skeptical, saying the suggestion that she fell out of a tree is largely a ‘just-so story’ that is neither verifiable nor falsifiable, and therefore unprovable. The new research focused on “a small subset of fractures” that are consistent with “high-energy bone-to-bone impacts” and which differ from the sorts of breaks commonly seen in fossilised bones, the researchers said. “It is ironic that the fossil at the center of a debate about the role of arborealism in human evolution likely died from injuries suffered from a fall from a tree,” Dr. John Kappelman, a professor of anthropology and geological sciences at the university, said in a written statement. The researchers concluded that Lucy, who is believed to have stood about 3 feet 6 inches and weighed about 60 pounds, fell feet first and used her arms to brace herself.

text: A wooden canoe that scientists say could be hundreds of years old has emerged from the bottom of the Indian River along Florida’s eastern coast. If it is determined to be historic, the canoe will be stabilized, preserved and hopefully it will ultimately be displayed locally for the public to enjoy and learn from, the office said. The state has the highest concentration of archaeological dugouts in the world with more than 400 from the state, according to the U.S. Department of Archaeological Research, which sent an archaeologist over to examine the find on Thursday. It has been placed back in a wet environment in order to preserve the item, which has several uncommon features, including compartments, what appears to be a seat, and its nails. The nails were first in production in the early 19th century so that helps to indicate it is a historic canoe, a spokeswoman for the office told ABC News. It's not especially unique because of the high number of dugout canoes found in the state; some have been found dating back to ancient times, others have been used and recreated in recent years.

That number goes up to 38 percent for the 18- to 34-year-old demographic. This might be the right move for the NFL if they want to hold on to younger viewers. The new NFL package will be free for subscribers, but Amazon already offers Prime members the ability to add special subscription packages, such as Showtime and Starz, for an additional price. “We’re focused on bringing our customers what they wants to watch, Prime members want the NFL,” Amazon Senior Vice President Jeff Blackburn told The Wall Street Journal. The NFL had a similar deal with Twitter last year for only $10 million dollars. The deal is expected to be in place for the start of the 2014 season. It is not clear if the NFL will continue to have a streaming service in the future, or if it will focus on just one channel at a time, like it did in the past when it had a streaming deal with DirecTV and satellite providers such as satellite giant satellite provider Dish.

text: Primo Levi was captured by the Fascist militia in December of 1943. He was sent to a detention camp at Fossoli. Two months later he was loaded onto a train for expatriation from the Republic. It is far from a heroic description of his “survival in Auschwitz,” writes Nicholas Heron. But it does so by bringing to light the existence of a distinct oppositional pair much less evident in ordinary life: the drowned (i sommersi) and the saved (i salvati) In Auschwitz, all the ritual humiliations appeared as if designed to hasten the prisoner's descent to what Levi termed “the bottom”. But this process was especially accelerated in the case of those he called the drowned: “they followed the slope down to the bottom, like streams that run down to sea” These were the prisoners who, for whatever reason, adjusted to the brutal regimen of life in the camp; yet whose time was apparently endless. In the jargon of the camp, these were the Muselmänner, the “Muslims” whose tenuous existence, even prior to their imminent selection for the gas chamber, hovered in an indistinct between life and death.

text: HD 20782b is located 117 light-years away and was first discovered in 2006. The planet is about the size of Jupiter but has an orbit like an ellipse. The researchers aren't sure how the planet ended up in such a bizarre orbit. They hope to continue their observations in the future to get a closer look at what exactly is happening when the planet makes its closest approach to its star."Finding more of these kinds of planets" will hopefully allow us to answer that question, Dr. Stephen Kane told The Huffington Post. "It is a fascinating object!" the astronomer said of the exoplanet's eccentric orbit, which is similar to that of a comet or an asteroid. "The notion that a giant planet could exist in such extreme conditions is difficult to imagine," Kane said. "Myself and my collaborators spent several years studying the object further to find out if the situation is as extreme as we initially thought," he added. "What we found is that, not only is the orbit the most eccentric ever found, the planet shows strong evidence of flashing reflected starlight at us whenever it makes its close approach to the star," he said. The study was released online before print and is slated to be published in The Astrophysical Journal, a journal of the American Astronomical Society. "When we see a planet like this that is in an eccentric orbit ... it can be really hard to try and explain how it got that way," Kane says. "We will learnHow the planet heats up and cools down again and find out whether this process is stripping the atmosphere away from the planet"

The Great Lakes hold nearly one-fifth of the surface fresh water in the world and are home to about 1.5 billion people, or one-quarter of the population in the United States and about one-tenth of the world's population. text: A new wildlife corridor will connect fragmented habitats. Funding has been secured for a 10-year conservation initiative. The Sea otter faces serious threats to its survival, but conservationists are taking action. It is estimated that the sea otter population in the UK is less than 1,000. The species is threatened by habitat loss, over-fishing and habitat fragmentation. It has been listed on the endangered species register for more than 30 years, and its population has declined by more than 80 per cent since the 1970s. It was listed as threatened by the Endangered Species Act in 1973, and listed as endangered by the World Wildlife Fund in 1986. It's estimated that only about 1,500 sea otters remain in the wild today, and they are in need of protection from habitat loss and over-collection. The population is estimated to be less than 100,000, and this is expected to fall to as little as half by the end of the century. The current population is thought to be between 10 and 20 years old, and it is expected that it will fall to less than 50,000 by the time of the next population census in 2035. The conservationists hope to protect the population by creating a new corridor to link fragmented habitats, allowing populations to interact and strengthen genetic diversity. The new corridor will cost around £1.5 million.

The finding is somewhat surprising. text: 500 chatbots read the news from July 1, 2020, and discussed what they had read. The scientists had used ChatGPT 3.5 to build the bots for a very specific purpose. It's difficult to model something like Twitter — or to do any kind of science, really — using actual humans.. AI bots, on the other hand, will do whatever you tell them to, practically for free. And their whole deal is that they are designed to act like people. Researchers are starting to use chatbots as fake people from whom they can extract data about real people. By replacing people as the subjects in scientific experiments, AI could conceivably turbocharge our understanding of human behavior in a wide range of fields, from public health and epidemiology to economics and sociology. The idea of populating made-up social networks with digital proxies goes back even further. In 2006, researchers at Columbia Universitybuilt an entire social networkto study how 14,000 human users shared and rated music.

text: Denver experiment gives homeless people straight-up cash with no strings attached. Six months in, most who received money from the project were better off. Those that received $500 or more per month saw the biggest gains. The number sleeping in shelters was more than halved, and all reported increased feelings of safety in their current sleep location, researchers say. The study also relied on participants self-reporting their situations in exchange for payments of up to $30. But the findings track with other cities' experiences, such as in San Francisco, where two-thirds of those who were homeless at the start had found permanent housing six months after the experiment began.. Other countries are also finding that the carrot of direct cash assistance is a more effective means of addressing poverty than either social assistance or the stick of policing or the patronization of more traditional assistance programs, where aid comes with more strings attached, a professor of psychology at the University of British Columbia told The Guardian. "Housing improved, reduced homelessness, increased spending and savings over time, and was a net savings for government and taxpayers," Jiaying Zhao, an associate professor, said.

The movie, while told from Jamie’s point of view, belongs to Dorothea, and Bening, who outshines an impressive cast. The plot is subdued, and at times meandering, but the stakes are low in the film, which is about Bening's loosening off of domestic shackles and her attempt to raise a young man who's a feminist ally, in the throes of the movement's second wave. It's unlikely that the movie's less progressive conception was its downfall in the eyes of the Academy, which has been criticized for favoring the narratives of those with power to those without it. But it wouldn't be a jump to think that “20thcentury Women’ was overlooked due to what some critics count as its strength: it’re a moodpiece, not the high-Volume, c Rescendoing Drama or Musical of the past few years. It is an autobiographical reflection of the Coppola-like tendency to shroud every scene in a shroud of light, regardless of its subject matter. No matter which side you fall on, it's evident that Mills’ storytelling techniques neatly match the stories he sets out to tell. He uses meandering scenes in diffuse light, like projector slides, an effect some critics find authentic, and others find gratuitously twee.

text: Anew study, published by KAUST researchers inNature Communications, shows that corals, jellyfish, and other symbiotic cnidarians control their symbiotic algae by limiting the amount of nitrogen available for proliferation. Findings disrupt traditional views of cooperative symbiosis in corals and have important implications for major coral reef restoration efforts such as the KAust Reefscape Restoration Initiative. By tracking nutrient exchange using carbon and nitrogen isotopes, the study shows how three different species have independently evolved this common mechanism for symbiosis withmarine algae(dinoflagellates) The researchers found that more ammonium promotes the algaepopulation sizebecause of the greater access to nitrogen, while more glucose reduces the population size since glucose promotes the ability of the host to assimilate more of its nitrogen waste. This knowledge will likely inspire further investigations into the regulatory mechanisms governing these relationships and inform policy-making to develop effective restoration strategies. The symbiosis is so strong that the algal symbionts live inside the hosts' cells.

text: This year is "virtually certain" to be the warmest in 125,000 years, European Union scientists say. Last month smashed through the previous October temperature record, from 2019, by a massive margin. Globally, the average surface air temperature in October was 1.7 degrees Celsius warmer than the same month in 1850-1900. The heat is a result of continued greenhouse gas emissions from human activity, combined with the emergence this year of the El Nino weather pattern, which warms the surface waters in the eastern Pacific Ocean. "We must not let the devastating floods, wildfires, storms, and heatwaves seen this year become the new normal," said Piers Forster, climate scientist at University of Leeds. The only other time before October a month breached the temperature record by such a large margin was in September 2023, according to the EU's Copernicus Climate Change Service. "September really, really surprised us. So after last month, it's hard to determine whether we're in a new climate state," said C3S Deputy Director Samantha Burgess.

And what this piece has been teaching me is what our main challenge in being human is. If all sounds arise from the soul, then all sounds must be treated equally. Healing and personal transformation with integration and integration with each other is what this work is teaching me. And from our shared shared experience, we have shared the beautiful and beautiful and low, the low, and the high, the beautiful, the high and the low and the beautiful. We have begun to perceive parts, the divine parts, that I have begun perceive as viscerally a place within me. text: Ed Yong: The mirror test is one of the most famous techniques in the study of animal intelligence. The test has been administered to dozens of species, and usually takes roughly the same form. Other clever creatures have largely or completely failed the test, including crows, parrots, gorillas, monkeys, dogs and even some young children. But these failures say very little about whether these individuals have a sense of self, and a lot about whether the Mirror test is actually appropriate for them, he says. He says the test is a visual test, designed by visual animals (us) for other visual animals. It makes little sense to confront them with a mirror. You need to work in their world. A world of chemicals drifting through the air, hard for us to imagine. It’s taken a long time to see — or even imagine — what the world might be like for non-visual creatures, and to design experiments with that in mind,” says Alexandra Horowitz from Barnard College. She recruited 36 New York dog owners and presented their pooches with two canisters. In one, she put a tiny drop of each dog's own urine. In the other, she placed the same urine along with a different scent. The dogs spent more time sniffing the canister with the modified odor than the one with their unadulterated urine. The presence of the extra scent changed how they behaved toward their own smell, just as the presence of a red mark changes how a chimp behaves toward its image.

text: Brachial plexus birth injury (BPBI) or Erb’s palsy is a relatively uncommon injury (1 to 2 in every 1000 babies) that occurs to a newborn baby during the process of vaginal delivery. Prolonged and difficult labour along with larger baby size are the most common risk factors. Twin births, use of vacuum or forceps during delivery and breech delivery also increase the chances of developing this condition. The severity of the injury varies according to the pattern of nerves affected and the type of injury to each nerve. Nerves can be stretched, ruptured, or torn away from the spinal cord. In cases of a mild nerve stretch, complete recovery occurs within 6 to 8 weeks after birth. In case of more severe injuries, spontaneous recovery is less likely and surgery to reconnect the nerves may be required. In older children who are unable to use the arm or shoulder, muscle release and tendon transfer surgery can be performed with good results. It is advisable for all children with brachialplexus injury to take up swimming, dancing and sports.

text: Scientists in Australia are aiming a huge dish telescope at Proxima Centauri, one of our close solar neighbors. The Parkes Radio Telescope in New South Wales will lend a hand, er, dish to the mix, scanning for radio frequencies that might originate from unknown civilizations in space. This is Australia’s first collaboration with Breakthrough Listen, a 10-year, $100 million global effort to actively search for intelligent alien life. The project's international supporters include Stephen Hawking, Frank Drake, Lord Martin Rees, and Ann Druyan, co-author of the “Cosmos” television programs and widow of astronomer Carl Sagan. Locating a verifiable intelligent alien radio signal is basically like looking for a cosmic needle in a haystack, but scientists believe Earth's most powerful telescopes are the best chance of helping to answer the question of whether earthlings are alone in the universe. “I think it is actually real science, even though the chance of success is small,” program director for Commonwealth Scientific and Industrial Research Organization John Reynolds said. But no matter what, he added, the search effort isn’t pointless. "I’m a bit of a skeptic, but I like the idea,’ Reynolds said, “it’S definitely a question that has to be answered, and you won't find out unless you actually look.” The video below is an artist's illustration, showing how the Parkes Telescope “looked” through dust and gas of our Milky Way galaxy and found nearly 900 galaxies.

text: Neurological disorders have become a growing concern, affecting millions of people worldwide. These disorders encompass a wide spectrum of conditions concerning the nervous system, including the brain, spinal cord, and nerves. Identifying a neurological disorder can be a complex task, as the symptoms can vary widely from one disorder to another. The treatment approach may vary depending on the specific disorder and its severity. Some disorders can be managed with medication and therapy, while others may require surgery or other specialized interventions. For example, neurosurgeries are broadly divided into traditional and minimally invasive keyhole neurosurgery. Minimally invasive techniques employ smaller incisions, specialized tools, and advanced imaging. The result is reduced trauma, minimal scarring, quicker recovery, shorter hospital stays, and lessoperative discomfort. The reduced risk of complications is also noteworthy, Dr. Mohana Rao Patibandla said. For more information, visit Dr. Rao's Hospital's Neurosurgery and Neurology Department. text: When The Earth Trembled, or The Strength of Love, is one of the earliest three-reelers from the silent era. On May 29, the San Francisco Silent Film Festival presented the American premiere of the long-lost 1913 film. The film won the Pulitzer Prize for Drama in 2010 and received its world premiere from the Steppenwolf Theatre Company in Chicago in 2010. It was recently directed by Josh Costello, who recently directed the Bay Area premiere of Detroit's Aurora Theatre Company's The Glass Menagerie, which opened in New York City in May. The full title of the film indicates that there is far more woe in store for the protagonist than a 7.8 earthquake. It took O' Neil nearly four months to design and create the special effects that could recreate that horrible day. The San Francisco earthquake was only a small part of the melodramatic plot crammed into a three- reel drama into which a lot of family drama was crammed. It is thought that some actors narrowly escaped being severely injured during the earthquake scenes (a chandelier fell on Ethel Clayton as she was trying to escape from a collapsing house) The film was considered lost for many years (largely because, on June 13, 1914, a fire had destroyed all the negatives produced by the Lubin Manufacturing Company since its launch in 1896) However, on March 28, 2015, the EYE Film Institute Netherlands presented the world premiere of a digitally restored version of When The EarthTrembled.

text: Stephen Hawking co-authored a paper about the existence of parallel universes. The study was published in the Journal of High-Energy Physics posthumously. It suggests that these alternate universes are subject to the same laws of physics as our own. Hawking died at the age of 76 on March 14, due to complications from amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, a progressive neurodegenerative disease. He rose to global fame in 1988, after publishing a general audience book on science, A Brief History of Time. His ashes will be interred inside London’s Westminster Abbey later this year, near the graves of scientists Isaac Newton and Charles Darwin. The British physicist is best known for his theories on black holes. He also has at least two other papers that are being prepared for publication, according to the Guardian. The paper uses new mathematical techniques to restore order to previously chaotic views of the multiverse, suggesting that these different universes are Subject to the Same Laws of Physics as Our Own. The physicists also gave other researchers a pathway to potentially detect the presence of other universes by searching for cosmic microwave radiation that is left over from the Big Bang. They drew on 20 years of work, and the study was submitted to the open-access journal shortly before Hawking's death, the BBC reported. It was unclear to them whether the laws of Physics that apply in our universe would also apply in these alternate universe. "The mystery was why do we live in this special universe where everything is nicely balanced in order for complexity and life to emerge?” said co-author Thomas Hertog.

text: Antarctic sea ice covers an area the size of Antarctica itself. But this year there was less ice than ever before, going back to when satellites started tracking annual ice extent around 1980. Disappearing sea ice is a problem for lots of reasons. It doesn't directly add any extra water to the ocean, but missing sea ice does contribute to global sea level rise in other ways. The sea ice around Antarctica shields glaciers on land, and massive ice shelves that extend out into the water. Without that protection, that ice can melt more quickly, and that leads to more sea levels rise.. The West Antarctic ice shelf is the part of Antarctica that is melting most rapidly in response to climate change. It contains enough water to raise global sea levels by about 10 feet. And it is not too late to protect the entire West Antarctica ice sheet. But scientists expect East Antarctica to remain relatively stable for 100 years, or more, as more warm water mixes with the ice. The East Antarctic ice sheet is likely to stay stable.

text: The official start date for winter can be a bit confusing. The meteorological calendar offers the most accurate insights from which informed decisions can be made for the safety of people, products and property. This year is proving to be interesting as we head into winter with what was already a strong El Niño event getting even stronger. With El Niño firmly in place and remaining at least the first half of winter, much of North America will see above-normal temperatures. The main storm track will be from California across the Southern Plains into the Southeast. The coldest 90-day period in the U.S. begins before December 1 across the country's Southwestern region and after December 1 in the Northeastern region. The data also shows that for every location in the lower 48 states, the coldest 60 days of the year always begins within 12 days of December 1. If you average the temperatures in cities across the continental U.s., the coldiest 90- day period starts on November 30. It’s also worth noting that there is no city in which astronomical winter is colder than meteorological winter.

The blog also shared the image of an annular eclipse, also known as a “ring of fire.” The blog says the phenomenon is caused by the Earth’s atmosphere absorbing some of the Sun's light, creating an ill-defined edge. text: Madagascar is rich in species found nowhere else on Earth. When humans began settling on the island about 2,300 years ago, giant tortoises disappeared. Researchers think they've found a way to replace Madagascar's lost giant tortoise species. They plan to transplant a very close relative of the extinct giant Tortoises to Madagascar to help fill the ecological gaps left by their extinct kin."This will open fantastic perspectives for conservation in Madagascar," says biologist Miguel Pedrono. "Of course, any time you introduce a species, there are many potential pitfalls," says ecologist Elizabeth Hunter, of the University of Georgia. "This plan is cautious and will allow researchers to discover those before anything goes too wrong," Hunter says of the plan. "I would fully support going forward with this plan," Hunter said. "Visitors" on the Mascarene Island of Rodrigues are restoring the island's tortoise-replacement scheme, Pedrona says.. The project could also be a boon for Madagascar's ecotourism industry, he says. For more information on the project, visit LiveScience's LiveScience page. The team plans to move 300 young tortoise to a nature reserve in western Madagascar, where they'll live in an enclosed pen for five years. They'll be monitored for eating habits and other ecological interactions before they can breed and disperse across the island. It's likely that ancestors of the giant tortaises living on Aldabra Atoll made the 249-mile (400 kilometers) swim from Madagascar about 100,000 years ago.

text: Scientists from six countries conducted a field experiment on three tropical mountains. They offered ants different food sources in order to find out which nutrients these important insects prefer most in nature. The results led to the discovery of more than 100 undescribed species of ants. The number of ants significantly declined towards higher, cooler locations, where their foraging activity decreased by approximately 25% for every 500 meters of elevation. On all continents, more predatory ant species were observed towards the mountaintops, while species feeding on sweet honeydew and nectar were more abundant in the lowlands. The reason may be that in thedry seas of South America, there are more species outside the rainy season, while nectar-feeding species should lack amino acids and salts, while sugars in their diet should be more plentiful in the high mountains. The study was published in the journalGlobal Ecology and Biogeography, by Petr Klimes and Yvonne Tiede of the Biology Center of the Czech Academy of Sciences.

text: Global average temperature on Friday was more than 2 degrees Celsius hotter than levels before industrialization. The threshold was crossed just temporarily and does not mean that the world is at a permanent state of warming above 2 degrees. But it is a symptom of a planet getting steadily hotter and hotter, and moving towards a longer-term situation where climate crisis impacts will be difficult — in some cases impossible — to reverse. The breach of 2 degrees on Friday came two weeks before the start of the UN COP28 climate conference in Dubai, where countries will take stock of their progress towards the Paris Climate Agreement pledge to limit global warming to 1.5 degrees. A UN report last week found that even if countries carried out their current emissions-reduction pledges, the world would reach between 2.5 and 2.9 degrees of warming sometime this century. Warming to 2 degrees puts far more of the population at risk of deadly extreme weather and increases the likelihood of the planet reaching irreversible tipping points, such as the collapse of the polar ice sheets.

text: Artists who make graphic prints or sculpture editions usually look to print studios or foundries. The decision on which foundry or print studio to use is complicated by issues of location, price, the right fit of services and the media available. Fees may be based on an hourly rate or for the entire project, with payment made at the end, usually within 30 days of completion. Rejection or cancellation prior to the completion of an edition usually entails a kill fee of 50 percent; if the edition is completed, the artist will be expected to pay the full agreed-upon amount. The artist may not like the work that the studio staff is doing, or there may be a reason that the whole project has to be cancelled. It is not uncommon for studios to tack on interest charges -- for instance, one-and-a-half percent per month or an annualized 18 percent -- for late payments. The cost of producing a single object or an edition is determined based in part on what the foundry is asked to do -- make molds, build a supporting structure, cast the piece, patinate, install the finished work, transport and store molds and insure the molds. The first thing that sculptors should ask for is a quote that is in the range of a change of order, because alterations are likely to be made during the design or fabrication process. Since material and labor costs fluctuate, the quote should have a 90-day lifespan, with another 30 percent paid at some point at completion.

Thecenter will not be open to the public and is not expected to open until at least 2015. The first four elephants arrived at the center in May and are expected to live there for at least five years, the center's website says. The elephants will live in an ideal environment, including watering holes, areas to wallow in mud and areas to play in the mud. The facility is expected to be open for up to five years. It will be funded by donations from zoos, wildlife organizations, foundations and private donors, the Center's website states. It is located on a plot of land that is currently owned by the Florida Department of Agriculture and Florida Fish and Wildlife. It's not clear how much the center will cost, but it's expected to cost about $10 million to $20 million to build and maintain. text: "Behavioral contagion" is a well-documented phenomenon in psychology. Our brains are hardwired for social interaction and bonding. Contagious yawning is a sign of empathy and a form of social bonding. Just looking at a person who's cold can be enough to make you feel too, according to a study from Brighton and Sussex Medical School. A study conducted by neuroscientists at the California Institute of Technology finds that after we witness others engaging in financially risky behavior, we in turn are more likely to take similar risks. The same instinct that leads us to smile when others do also gives us the impulse to turn down the corners of our mouths when we see someone else frowns. The study suggests that when we're with a person and they smile, we're likely to "try on" that facial expression to get a sense of how they're feeling. But there's one type of person who seems to be completely immune to the contagion effect of yawning: psychopaths, whose personalities are marked by the inability to feel empathy, don't "catch" yawns like the rest of us. It's said that when you smile, the whole world smiles with you -- and psychologists have shown that this common cliche contains a kernel of truth. A 2015 study from the University of Florida, published in the journal Applied Psychology, found that when people encounter rude behavior at work, they're more Likely to perceive rudeness in future workplace interactions, and in turn to respond rudely themselves.

text: Footprints from ice-age humans some 13,000 years ago have been found beneath the sands of a Canadian Island in the Pacific. The first North Americans are widely believed to have crossed from Siberia to Alaska via a Bering land bridge. The footprints suggest the early travelers then may have traveled south along the Pacific coast, rather than farther inland. The prints, found during excavations from 2014 to 2016, also suggest the humans may havetraveled among islands via primitive boats, though no evidence of boats has been found. The findings add to the “growing body of evidence that early peoples in the Americas inhabited the coastal margin and circumnavigated the western edge of the Cordilleran Ice Sheet to move between Beringia [the land bridge] and mid-latitude North America at the end of the last ice age,” the authors wrote in the journal PLOS One. The few archeological sites discovered previously as far north were slightly earlier, from 12,700 to 11,800 years ago, according to Ars Technica. The earliest boat is a dugout canoe in the Netherlands dated about 10,000 year ago. The. footprints provide “evidence of the seafaring people who inhabited this area during the tail end ofthe last major ice age," said Duncan McLaren, lead author of the study.

text: Aerosol particles influence the climate in two ways: first, by directly affecting how much sunlight ends up on the surface of Earth, and second, through the formation of clouds. Accounting for these experimental findings in models can better predict howhuman activityaffects air quality and the climate. Once the models are more accurate, they predict better the interrelated effects of various human perturbations to the climate system, says postdoctoral researcher Runlong Cai from the Institute for Atmospheric and Earth System Research INAR at the University of Helsinki. The latest experimental results provide much better understanding of the formation and growth of various particles, yet they cannot be applied as effectively as possible in climate models, as their precise modeling requires too much computing power, says University Researcher Juha Kangasluoma from INAR. The study was published in theReviews of Modern Physicsjournal.

text: Study: Physical exercise can help people retain information if it happens at the right time. Researchers divided 72 people into groups and then had them all complete a memory task. The findings offer initial evidence that properly timed physical exercise can improve memory retention, the authors say. The study tested the effects of exercising after a four-hour delay, but it's possible that waiting two hours or six hours to exercise could have a better (or worse) effect on memory."Physical exercise is at the start of this sequence, because it is accompanied by the release of dopamine and norepinephrine," Fernandez said. The researchers speculate this may be the reason why exercising helped the people in their study to retain information, which would otherwise be lost. "These proteins help stabilizing new memory traces," Fernandez told The Huffington Post, "which would otherwise been lost," he said. It's also possible that high-intensity exercise is "likely necessary" to produce the memory-improving effects.

It wasn't until the bits of signage and text included in European Cubist pictures began to nudge Stuart Davis and a few others to bring stylized words into their canvases that the old marriage ofWords and images could be truly reborn in American art, writes Taylor. It's interesting to note that things developed differently in Asia and the Islamic world, where calligraphy remained revered and essential. In China, where children still learn to write with a brush, the literati ideal of poetry and image being conjoined is still strong. So is the idea that a landscape can be a mindscape. Until photography came along, art images were windows through which we could witness things, and be moved by their validating realness. After the war, in the era of Pop art, when culture replaced nature as art's dominant subject matter, words no longer had to knock at the door of culture and ask to be let in.

text: Milan Kundera’s new novel, The Festival of Insignificance, is one of these late-career bad books. With a startling relish, writers from The New York Times and The Guardian have denounced the slim hundred-pager as out-of-touch, sexist, and, worst of all, banal. Yet there's good reason to ponder the book. Not destined to be a masterpiece, it nevertheless remains ripe for a different sort of analysis. It's disappointing that so few of the reviews have dug into the philosophical meat of the new novel -- because it diverges so drastically from earlier Kunder a works. The Festival is a complete embrace of the lightness KunderA once seemed to reject. It is a question of whether the novelist of ideas radically changed his own ideas of lightness when he left behind his homeland, opting for the very very life of Parisians in the very garden of the very life he once lived in Prague. The book is more than a book. It has become intertwined with the writer's cultural legacy and personal history. It began with the ardently anti-communist The Joke in 1967, shed its political bent after The Unbearable Lightness of Being, then switched languages from Czech to French after 1990. If a shallow late-novel recalls and complicates those decades of depth, is it really so shallow? It's difficult to lapse into nihilism when there are pressing issues like political catastrophe to attend to. Lightness, the characters found out, was the truly awful condition.

'I" is the first person pronoun of the ﬁrst person in English, while in some other languages it is the second person that is honoured by this distinction, Otto Jespersen wrote more than 100 years ago. The Asian male, born in China but an immigrant at an early age to America, perceives what nobody else does, that camping is more than setting up a tent in the woods. To him, camping is about who owns those woods — and by extension, his wife. Harm could be considered part of a recent series of cautionary tales about inviting people over for a meal. God of Carnage (a global blockbuster for Yasmina Reza in 2008) and Disgraced (Ayad Akhtar”s Pulitzer Prize winner, the most produced play of 2016), two other recent Broadway hits, demonstrated in detail how dinner parties can descend into hell or at least purgatory. The play is about, as many plays end up being about, its own language. It's about whether people mean what they say and say what they mean, and the consequences that follow. Underneath the camping, there is race, but underneath race, there are domestic conflict twice over. And, at the end of the tension, of course, the invitation to smooth over all of the tensions, by camping. It’S too late by then. We think we are talking about camping. But really we’re talking about race.

The study was conducted on ice cores previously obtained by Ohio State University paleoclimatologist Lonnie Thompson who has been visiting the Peruvian glacier since the early 1960s. The research showed that the Qori Kallis outlet glacier, part of the bigger ice cap, extended to its maximum position about 520 years ago. It then retreated and has since had only minor re-advances. The researchers compared the sediment with the ice core record and determined that temperature changes drove the glacial expansions and retreats. "This result agrees with Professor Thompson's earlier suggestions that these tropical glaciers are shrinking very rapidly today because of a warming climate," study co-author Meredith Kelly said in a press release. The New York Times also interviewed other scientists who have studied glaciers. One praised it, while another believed the findings but said he didn't "see that they make a compelling case," according to the Times. text: John Gyakum and Fred Sanders coined the term "bomb cyclone" in 1980. They used the phrase to describe powerful cyclones that get their energy from rapid drops in pressure. About 40 bomb cyclones can occur off the northern Atlantic and Pacific coasts each year, according to the National Weather Service. Despite the planet overall warming, northern regions have been hit with a growing number of extreme cold snaps over the past four decades, research shows. The number of bomb cyclone events is twice as fast as the rest of the planet, scientists say. But climate change threatens to make them stronger and more frequent, they say. The Washington Post published an article Tuesday afternoon comparing the storm to a winter hurricane, warning that winds could reach 70 mph in some parts of New England. It was the first use of the term “bomb” in 1964 by Sanders, a professor of synoptic meteorology at Massachusetts Institute of Technology. He died in 2006 at age 83, and is now considered the father of theterm “Bomb cyclone.’’ Gyakums said he avoids using the term himself, but hopes its newfound popularity will raise awareness about the dangers of bomb Cyclone events. He said he hopes the term will be used to raise awareness of the danger of bomb Cyclones in the future, as well as other extreme weather events like hurricanes and other major weather events.

text: It's been 2,880 days since Hurricane Wilma made landfall in the United States. That's twice as long as any major hurricane landfall "drought" since 1915. The reasons behind this drought turn out to be a combination of atmospheric wind patterns, how close to the coast hurricanes form and luck. "It's just a fluke, and good luck," said one meteorologist with the Washington Post's Capital Weather Gang blog. "Our time will come again," said Brian McNoldy, a researcher at the University of Miami. "We certainly haven't been in a quiet pattern," said another meteorologist. "I am in the camp that this is a natural variation and that over time it will average back out," said Jeff Weber, a scientist with the University Corporation for Atmospheric Research in Boulder, Colo. "There's not enough data to make this statistically significant," another scientist said, adding that it's too short a period to make any assumptions based on this statistic."I'd say it's mostly luck," the National Hurricane Center's Chris Landsea said. "Most hurricanes that have approached have turned back," he added. "But that's something that's extremely variable, and not predictable," Landsea added."It's not like the last eight years have been quiet. Seven hurricanes, for example, have made landfall" in the U.S. since 2005, government records show, but two of them were Category 2 storms, and the latter nearly became a major hurricane.

text: Dinosaurs were dying off tens of millions of years before an asteroid strike hastened their extinction. The sauropods, a group of dinosaurs that included long-necked species like Apatosaurus, were dying out the quickest. Scientists have long sought to settle a debate about the dinosaurs' vitality prior to obliteration. The research challenges recent theories that dinosaurs were flourishing 66 million years ago, when a massive asteroid collided with an area in present-day Mexico, resulting in the Chicxulub crater."It is clear that they were already past their prime in an evolutionary sense," lead paleontologist Manabu Sakamoto said in a statement. "I think if there was no asteroid you would still have dinosaurs around today," another scientist said, adding that the dinosaurs could have bounced back if the asteroid hadn't hit. "It may be that the effects of the asteroid were a bit worse because you had dinosaurs that maybe weren’t as strong as they once had been," Stephen Brusatte told The Guardian in a separate interview. The new study conflicts with a 2014 study that found no evidence of long-term decline in the dinosaurs, which had been thought to have thrived for about 50 million years before the asteroid hit the Yucatan peninsula in what is now the Mexico City area. The researchers reached their findings by conducting a statistical analysis and examination of the fossil record from when dinosaurs appeared 231 million years old to the time when they ceased to exist, they said.

"She had a normal pregnancy that lasted 340 days, and the foaling lasted less than 10 minutes," says a scientist at SCBI. text: Researchers found faint traces of memory formed during sleep even if the individuals themselves remained largely unaware of those memories. In the study, neuroscientists Thomas Andrillon and Sid Kouider of Paris’ Ecole Normale Superieure asked 22 participants to listen to an audio stream of words as they drifted into sleep. The words kept playing in their ears during the nap. Upon awakening, participants did not remember the words they had heard while asleep and couldn’t tell them apart from new words in a memory test. But using electroencephalography, which picks up on the brain’s electrical activity, the researchers found an implicit memory trace for words presented during sleep. Hearing those words after the nap triggered a EEG result different from that of completely new words. The finding that words heard in sleep leave a trace behind was corroborated by measuring participants’ confidence level in memory tests. When participants were asked if a certain word was presented to them during sleep, they expressed a bit more confidence in their answer when it was correctly yes — as if they had a hunch about that word. Still, that doesn't mean you can learn new information during sleep in any useful way. If anything, the memory traces were so weak that one could conclude the opposite: that it's really hard, if not impossible, to learn anything useful while sleep. In other words, the potential benefits of nighttime learning are not worth losing quality sleep over. But the new findings suggest that some minimal memory formation is possible.

text: The butterfly effect describes how the consequences of tiny perturbations can very quickly grow to have a major impact on a system's final outcome. In weather science, these fast growing uncertainties are most often related to convection and precipitation. But this initial variation grows much more slowly in AI systems than in reality, potentially making AI weather predictions unreliable. Currently, the butterfly effect is not the limiting factor in weather prediction, because atmospheric measurement errors are still large enough that the Butterfly effect is comparatively negligible. Scientists may also be able to improve AI algorithms, for example, by artificially generating additional training data to teach these algorithms the power of the butterfly Effect. The study was published inGeophysical Research Letters. It was written by Tobias Selz and G. C. Craig, and published in the journal of Atmospheric and Oceanic Research. The authors note that accuracy may vary in exceptional meteorological conditions. It does modelweatherin midlatitude conditions well with the current level of measurement error, though Selz & Craig note that.

text: NASA has sent samples of human sperm to the International Space Station to study how fertilization could happen in space. Earlier studies for other types of sperm have pinpointed a number of issues in space, including sperm from sea urchins and bulls. text: Solar winter, spanning approximately from Nov. 6 to Feb. 3, encapsulates the quarter of the year with the scantiest daylight hours. Seasonal lag, driven by the differing heat capacities of land and water, introduces a delay in temperature adjustments. Earth's vast water bodies, with their higher heat capacity, retain warmth from preceding seasons. This thermal inertia means that even as we navigate the darkest days, the chill of winter may not be felt in full force. While the days may be at their shortest, the full brunt of winter's icy grip may still be veiled by the lingering warmth of seasons past. Solar panels continue to generate electricity even in below-freezing weather. This is because solar panels convert the abundant light from the sun into energy, not relying on the sun's heat. text: Scientists have discovered the preserved tail of a tiny, 99-million-year-old feathered dinosaur. The delicately feathered 1.4-inch tail with bone and tissue intact was frozen in time in a piece of amber originally discovered in a mine in northern Myanmar. It was eventually found last year at a street market by paleontologist Lida Xing of Beijing’s University of Geosciences. They’re believed to be the first-ever non-avian dinosaur feathers found preserved in amber, which are providing a fascinating glimpse into the early evolution of feathers and flight. The specimen, nicknamed Eva, was likely the size of a sparrow at death, but would have grown to the sizes of an ostrich had she lived. The weak structure of the crude, early feathers that lack the interlocking architecture of ones developed up the evolutionary ladder was also not conducive to flight, according to the researchers. The feathers are missing a strong central shaft, known known as a rachis, which may have provided temperature regulation or some kind of signal, the scientists speculate. "It's a spectacular little glimpse. It gives us, basically, a pathway that gets us to modern feathers," said Ryan McKellar of Canada”s Royal Saskatchewan Museum, who helped lead the research. The tail belonged to a juvenile coelurosaur, part of the family of theropod dinosaurs related to Tyrannosaurus rex as well as others that developed into modern birds.

text: Self-propelled microbots could remove up to 95 percent of lead from water in an hour. Lead is commonly found in wastewater from mines or factories that make batteries and electronic devices. Heavy metal pollution can cost big cities billions of dollars a year. The bots are composed of three layers. The outer layer is made of graphene oxide to absorb heavy metals, while a middle layer makes the microbots ferromagnetic so they can be steered by external magnets."In my opinion, we should see first commercial use of self-pro propelled microbots in the next couple of years," co-author Samuel Sánchez says."Microbots" smaller than the width of a human hair could be highly effective and cost-efficient tools for removing lead and other contaminants from industrial wastewater, according to a new study published in the journal Nano Letters last month. The microbots aren't ready for open water, so they would swim in "a controlled environment, such as small reservoirs, pipes, containers," the study says. "This technique is scalable, so we envision that small companies could use microbots to decontaminate their water in case they cannot afford bringing their waste water," SánChez says, adding that the process could be scaled up to a large number of water treatment plants. "We envision using the microbot for the pre-treatment of industrial wastewater before dumping into a river," he says. The process could also be recycled, making the process even more efficient, he adds.

text: The lowercase letter "g" has two forms: the "opentail" one most people use, and the "looptail" form commonly seen in print and online in fonts such as Times New Roman and Calibri. Researchers from Johns Hopkins University found that while everyone can read the looptail g just fine, most people can’t write it or even correctly identify when it’s on its own. In another experiment, only 2 of 38 adults named “g” when they were asked to list letters with two lowercase forms, and only one could write both. “Our findings give us an intriguing way of looking at questions about the importance of writing for reading,” senior author Michael McCloskey said in a news release. "Here is a naturally occurring situation where, unlike most letters, this is a letter we don't write," he said. "We could ask whether children have some reading disadvantage with this form of g," he added. "This is not true of letters in general. What's going on here?” said cognitive science graduate student Gali Ellenblum. text: New paper crunches archive data from NASA's Cassini spacecraft, which orbited Saturn from 2004 to 2017. It reveals how much light the rings absorb. The study was published in the journal Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society, which is published by the British Astronomical Association, a division of the British Royal College of Astronomers, and the Royal Society of London, for which it is the editor-in-chief of the journal.

The traditional intention of photography to "represent the real" is actually a more physicalized way of recording something that "happened" in the first place. This work is inspired by a photographic impulse that that no longer needs to exist within a photographic realm. In a term I've used before, the Imagiatic (as opposed to the Photographic medium), the Imaginary doesn't really matter, all the intangible ideas that traditionally lived within photography don't need to be lived within a conceptual realm. The notion that there is any singular truth is a complete fiction, and defines the problem of history. History is, fundamentally, misremembering--it is gleaned from what one is told, what one reads, and what one learns and watches in film, not from whatOne experiences. The reality of experiences is more like a satellite structure, looking at a particular situation (the hotel spaces around the LAX airport, sites where various figures, fictional and real, have disappeared along the edge of the Pacific) from as many different viewpoints and strategies of dislocation as possible.

text: A new paper describes how CO2 could be mixed with a fluid electrolyte, generating electrical energy in the process. They say that using all of the CO2 from power plants, industrial factories and residences could generate more than 1.5 trillion kilowatts of electricity every year. That, according to the paper, is 400 times more energy than is generated annually by the Hoover Dam. But lead researcher Bert Hamelers told NBC News that this process could put to use energy that would otherwise be wasted, making power plants and other facilities more efficient and allowing them to produce more electricity without increasing their levels of CO3 emissions. The process doesn't actually consume the carbon dioxide. It just puts it to use, so the carbon carbon dioxide may still need to be captured in some way rather than released into the atmosphere. The team forced CO2 into water and other fluids. Two special membranes were placed on either side of the water, one of which the positive ions could pass through and another which the negative ions could passed through. This produced a flow of electrons between the two membranes which could be captured by an electrode. Voila, electricity. It could be scaled up and there are alternative approaches that could flip that equation.

text: Climate change is occurring much faster than species are changing. Some species have been able to meet the challenge with rapid evolutionary adaptation and other changes in behaviour or physiology. However, rapid adaptation to climate change often comes at a cost. Populations get smaller due to the deaths of individuals that cannot tolerate new, hotter temperatures. Even if species do evolve to survive with climate change, their smaller populations may still go extinct due to problems such as inbreeding, harmful new mutations or plain old bad luck, such as a disease epidemic. The rate of evolution is so mismatched to the rate of global warming that the study's authors estimate that nearly 70 per cent of the local populations they studied are already vulnerable to climate-driven extinction over the coming decades. The study found that the average species gained an average of 0.1 C (about 0.2 F) greater heat than all the other insect species over the world. At other times, his work is more intense, where the young woman seems impossible to see with her hair in such a way as to make it seem as if she is in a dream. The Tondo is a completely different situation. There is one endless side. And as a format, it has a much more focused configuration that has less to do with incorporating a background. My options are to either declare this one-up-up and toss a artificial tree, or seek out an organic tree or an artificial farm that doesn't use pesticides and fertilizers that I don't really want my baby crawling around in that, or keep my cat away from the tree, which is as easy as keeping the tree away from my baby. text: Erica Deeman photographs men of the African diaspora against a brown backdrop. The straightforward series addresses the omission of black men from the tradition of formal portraiture. The artist hopes her work can open up a broader narrative for men of color, as well as a more complex portrait of the human condition and the world around us. She does not want to influence her audience’s perception of her subjects, but rather leave space for the viewer to construct complex hypotheses regarding these strangers’ personalities. “I think photography is problematic because so many people see it as the truth,” Deeman said, “It has made people buy into physiognomy and eugenics and all of that.’” The work highlights the immense power of a simple ritual, a subject and photographer conspiring to create a portrait. For much of photography”s history, men of colour were denied access to self-portraits that truly represented themselves as complex individuals, she said. ‘In these photos, I’m saying: ‘This is how I think you should be seen, and this is how youshould be seen’ ’“I always joke that the photograph was the biggest lie that was ever made.”

Rosetta completed its free-fall descent at the speed of a sedate walk, joining the probe Philae, which landed on the comet in November 2014 in what was considered a remarkable feat of precision space travel. The mission managed several historic firsts, such as getting a spacecraft into orbit around a comet and the unprecedented landing of a probe on the surface of the icy comet. in March 2004, Rosetta launched from Earth and has been subjected to the harsh radiation and extreme temperatures of space since launching in May 2004. The ESA is ending the mission because 67P is racing toward the outer solar system, out of range for the solar-powered spacecraft, and so was unlikely to last too much longer. “It was a good ending,” Klaus Schiling, who worked on mission planning for Rosetta 27 years ago with prime contractor Airbus , told Reuters at the Mexico space conference. The images sent back from the Rosetta mission were “as powerful as Neil Armstrong’s first steps on the Moon,’ an astronomy expert said.

text: Scientists have found that archerfish can learn to recognize human faces with striking accuracy. In humans, the brain has a specialized region used for recognizing human faces, known as the fusiform face area, or FFA. The simpler brain of the fish entirely lacks this region, but it can learn subtle differences in visual patterns, the researchers say. The fish were able to do this task even when the faces were fairly similar, as you can see in the video below. In about 80 percent of the trials, the fish selected the face they already knew, according to the scientists at Oxford University. The archer fish have already demonstrated great vision by being able to detect small prey against a visually complex background, researchers said. Previous research has suggested that birds, and perhaps bees, are able torecognize human faces as well, the scientists said. The researchers say that if the archer Fish can tell humans apart, it's possible that other fish can, too. It's also possible that humans may have special facial recognition brain structures so that they can process a large number of faces very quickly or under a wide range of viewing conditions,” Cait Newport of Oxford University said. Of course, we humans are still better than fish at facial recognition, thanks to our F FA.

"The slower migration scenario that we ruled out might still be relevant in some cases," the paper's lead author says of the planet's orbit. "We can at least say that it is not the only way to produce a close-in planet," another astronomer says in an email. "No single discovery is going to answer all our questions about how the earth formed," a co-author says in the statement, but "it's important for understanding the formation of the earth and the origin" of life. "You might think of it as an infant," Trevor David, an astronomer atCaltech, said of the infant exoplanets. Plath died by suicide on February 11, 1963, leaving Hughes in control of her literary legacy, including her famous Ariel collection. Hughes claimed her journals from the years immediately preceding her death had been lost, later telling The Paris Review that he did destroy “one journal that covered maybe two or three months, the last months. And it was just sad. I just didn’t want her children to see it, no. Particularly her last days’ Hughes, who died in 1998, took pains to obscure or downplay his late wife’s more shocking journals and verses, saying “[s]he thought of her journals as working notes for some ultimate novel” rather than faithful accounts of her life. The claims allegedly made by Sylvia Plath [...] are as absurd as they are shocking to anyone who knew Ted well,” said Hughes’ widow, Carol Hughes, in a statement to The Guardian. text: Scientists have unveiled a miniature robotic stingray the size of a toenail. The bio-inspired robot is a made of a mixture of living rat heart cells and artificial material. It is only 16 millimeters long and weighs just 10 grams, or a third of an ounce. Just like stingrays and their Batoid relatives, the robot moves its flat body smoothly through water by flapping its fins in a wave-like motion. The movement of the fins is controlled by light pulses delivered to the heart muscles that line the surface of the robot's fins and is described in the journal Science on Thursday. The idea is to get a better insight into the human heart and heart disease by reverse engineering other muscular forms that we see in nature, the researcher said. He said the robot ray could interest scientists in a variety of fields, from the cardiac physiologist to the robotics engineer looking to use cells as a living engineering material. The team turned to optogenetics, a method often used in neuroscience studies as a way to switch neurons on and off with light. Applying a source of light to each fin allowed the researchers to stimulate the right or left fin and steer the robot in either direction. Different frequencies of light control how fast the fins, and hence the robot, move about. “That they got it to flap is wonderful. That they were able to steer it is nothing short of amazing,” said Adam Summers, director of the Comparative Vertebrate Biomechanics Lab at the University of Washington.

text: CTE has resulted in the deaths of more than 100 NFL players to date. CTE acts differently than other neurodegenerative disorders in that it is characterized by significant and often disturbing changes in behavior and mood. The suicides of several high-profile professional athletes, beginning with NFL player Terry Luther Long in 2005, brought CTE into the public consciousness. But despite a proliferation of cases, research into the mechanisms of this disease has only begun to reveal the true causes and potential effects. Despite almost a century of experience with the condition, the gaps in our knowledge are vast. Despite the real link between trauma and tau protein deposition, it is unlikely that an effective treatment will be developed without the real understanding of the real cause and effects of CTE. The risks of taking a piece of living brain to make a diagnosis are simply too high. Without a test for CTE that can be used in living individuals, research has been severely hamstrung. The most promising approach seems to be to use a special type of brain scan called positron emission tomography (PET). PET scans inject a radioactive tracer into an individual which is designed to bind to a specific substance in the body. In CTE, greater tau deposition is linked to greater number of concussions and more years of football playing, suggesting that repeated trauma is a precipitating event, but without understanding the real event, it's unlikely that it will be effective in treating the disease. It's a mystery as to what initiates this misfolding event.

text: Fire has scorched 15946 acres in Arizona. Residents who evacuated are being updated regularly on when it will be safe to return home. Community support centers are providing meals and supplies to displaced families. Air quality monitors show improvement in areas downwind of the fire. The fire has been burning since June 1 and has burned more than 1,000 acres. The cause of the wildfire is under investigation and no injuries have been reported. The blaze has been under control since June 2 and has charred more than 2,500 acres so far. The number of people affected by the fire is expected to rise as the day goes on, fire officials say. It is the second largest wildfire in the state since records began in 1998. The largest fire to burn in Arizona in more than 30 years, the fire has burned 1,200 acres since 2002. It has been dubbed the Rim Fire and is only 10% contained. The Firefighters Foundation has raised more than $100,000 to help fight the fire and provide relief to those affected by its spread. The American Red Cross has also raised $50,000 for the Arizona Firefighters Association. The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services has raised $30,000 so far this year to help with the fire's containment efforts. The National Weather Service has issued an air quality alert for parts of Arizona. The Air Quality Watchdog has also issued an alert for areas near the fire, which has burned over 1,100 acres since July 1.

text: A new study says the "hobbit" species of Flores Island may have lived 50,000 years ago. If true, that would mean H. floresiensis might have had contact with modern humans. Archaeologists first discovered fossilized skeletal remains of the species in 2003. A skull and limb bones indicated that a fully grown adult would have stood about 3.5 feet tall, and likely had an extremely small brain."We're just missing the evidence that we haven't discovered the sites that show exactly how modern humans navigated these islands to ultimately reach Australia," researcher says. "I see it as our responsibility to document our diversity," Dr. Matthew Tocheri says of the study's findings. "We still know very little" about the species, he says, "but there seems to be a debate over how much large or small their brain size was" and how it was re-organized in later life, he adds. "Over a third smaller than modern humans, even though it's so. reorganized, suggests that it was more. re- organized," he says of today's "Hobbits" The research suggests there was an entire lineage of hominins from Africa, Asia to the Indonesian island of Flores, so that scientists may have essentially missed out on the island's diversity, according to Tochersi, a paleoanthropologist at the Smithsonian Institution’s National Museum of Natural History. The study was published in the journal Nature on Wednesday.

text: Study: People perform better in intelligence tests if they expect brain-training games to help them. There's already growing debate over the efficacy of products that claim to train people's brains. Studies showing the brain-train games work may be inherently biased from selecting participants who expected to get smarter by playing brain games, says Cyrus Foroughi, co-author of the study. The burgeoning industry -- which was forecast to make $6 billion by 2020 -- is already taking hits, with the FTC fined the company behind the brain training program Lumosity $2 million in January for deceptive advertising. The FTC said the program “preyed on consumers’ fears about age-related cognitive decline,” and it “simply did not have the science to back up its ads.’‘The real reason behind people’s improvements in those studies should be accounting for self-selection bias and an important aspect of proper study design,’ Lumosity said in a statement to HuffPost. ‘The placebo effects in cognitive training is interesting and underscores the importance of properStudy design, suggesting that such as self- Selection bias and expectancy should be appropriately accounted for,‘ Forough i said. “Our scientists had 4,715 participants complete the study," the company said. "Half trained with Lumosity, while the rest did online crossword puzzles to control for placebo effects. After 10 weeks, the Lumosity group improved more than the crosswords group on an aggregate assessment of cognition”

text: Researchers at the Florida Institute of Technology filmed the video below. They're using a high-speed camera to capture amazing lightning flashes. "When current flows through an object, it can produce a lot of heat, which can really cause serious damage," he cautions everybody not to put themselves in harm's way as a storm approaches. "So, I don't want to be nearby any strike recorded on the video," Liu said. "Lightning is an electrical discharge process and we know, to start lightning, we need a very large electric field," he adds. "There is still debate about exactly how a cloud builds up electrical charges and how lightning forms," says the National Severe Storms Laboratory in Norman, Oklahoma. "Sometimes lightning can propagate upward from the thunder cloud tops. It can reach 60 to 70 kilometers [about 40 miles] into the low ionosphere," said Liu, referring to a conducting layer of the upper atmosphere that helps transmit radio signals around the world.
